text_blocks.snippet: Yes, COVID-19 can affect blood pressure. Studies have shown that COVID-19 can trigger new-onset high blood pressure, both in individuals hospitalized for the virus and those who were not. Specifically, people hospitalized for COVID-19 are more than twice as likely to develop persistent hypertension compared to those hospitalized with influenza, according to the American Heart Association. Furthermore, having pre-existing hypertension can increase the risk of severe COVID-19 illness or death.

text_blocks.snippet: To control high blood pressure immediately, focus on stress reduction techniques and potentially explore medication options. Deep breathing exercises and meditation can help lower blood pressure by reducing stress hormones. In cases of very high blood pressure (180/120 or above), seek immediate medical attention.
snippet_highlighted_words: focus on stress reduction techniques and potentially explore medication options

list.title: Deep Breathing:
list.snippet: Practice slow, deep breaths to activate your parasympathetic nervous system and calm your body.

list.title: Meditation:
list.snippet: Even short periods of meditation can help manage stress and lower blood pressure.

list.title: Warm Shower or Bath:
list.snippet: The warmth can help relax muscles and reduce tension, potentially lowering blood pressure.

list.title: Listen to Calming Music:
list.snippet: Music can be a powerful tool for relaxation and stress reduction.

list.title: Adjust Your Schedule:
list.snippet: Identify stressors in your schedule and try to create more space and time for relaxation.

list.title: Get Enough Sleep:
list.snippet: Lack of sleep can elevate blood pressure. Aim for a consistent sleep schedule.

list.title: Very High Blood Pressure:
list.snippet: If your blood pressure reaches 180/120 or higher, it's a medical emergency. Seek immediate medical attention.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: If you experience symptoms like chest pain, severe headache, or vision changes along with high blood pressure, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

list.title: Medication:
list.snippet: If you are prescribed medication for high blood pressure, take it as directed. It's the most effective way to lower blood pressure long-term.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: While not an immediate solution, long-term dietary changes can help manage blood pressure. Reducing sodium intake and incorporating fruits, vegetables, and whole grains can be beneficial, according to Northwestern Medicine.

list.title: Exercise:
list.snippet: Regular physical activity can help lower blood pressure over time, but for immediate impact, focus on stress-reducing exercises like walking or stretching.
